name: SkillCraft

scale.notes: 126 = tool-use tasks (21 task families x 6 scaled variants: 63 Easy, 42 Medium, 21 Hard; 3x3, 4x4, 5x5 entities x tool calls per entity). The repo matches (21 families, e1-e3/m1-m2/h1, counted 2026-10-10). There are no conversations. Modes: Base, Skill, Hierarchical, Cross-Task (Easy->Hard, Hard->Easy, Hard->Hard), and cross-model reuse.

metrics: Success Rate (rule-based task score >= 90%, overall and Hard subset)
Skill Exec Rate (successful skill executions / attempts)
Skill Reuse Rate (avg invocations per saved skill)
notes: Tests whether agents build a persistent library of executable "Skills" (composed tool calls) and reuse it within and across tasks. The task tools call live public web APIs (e.g. catfact.ninja, PokeAPI, Open-Meteo), so results may drift over time. Running it needs an LLM API key and Node.js/npx. The repo has no licence file. Within the paper, the domain count (6 vs. 8 domains in Table 5) and the per-level subtask counts (3/4/5 vs. 3/5/7) are inconsistent.

Trustworthiness compliance rate (overall, weighted by number of examples per dimension)
Per-dimension compliance: safety, robustness, truthfulness, privacy, fairness

Trust-Memevo data and trust-evaluation code are not released. The venue comes from the authors' README and homepage; the paper is not yet in ACL Anthology.

notes: Introduced alongside the STITCH memory method. Paper-result scripts are on the repo's paper-exp branch. arXiv comment says "ACL 2026"; ACL Anthology lists it in Findings.

name: Mem2ActBench

scale.notes: conversations = 2,029 long dialogue sessions built by merging ToolACE, BFCL and OASST1 conversations (abstract, §3.4.2, Table 1). questions = 400 memory-dependent tool-use tasks (abstract, §3.4.2, Table 1 'QA pairs'). The experiments (§4.1) do not use all 2,029 sessions. They use a 429-session subset that keeps only histories containing the QA evidence. This subset matches the repo's toolmembench_small/ folder (429 sessions, 400 QA, avg 3,422.5 tokens/session, 1,468,262 tokens total). The full folder Mem2ActBench/ has 2,029 sessions with 6,569,928 tokens total and 1,185-15,834 tokens per session. That folder also contains a 400-line qa_dataset.jsonl, but it is a different file from the one in toolmembench_small/ (the files differ). The average session length is reported three ways: 12 turns (abstract), 13 turns (Table 1, §3.4.2) and 12.67 turns (repo benchmark_statistics.json). Table 1's caption defines 'Tokens' as a total over all sessions, but its value of 3238 equals the repo's per-session average.

metrics: Tool Accuracy (TA: correct tool and all parameters match exactly)
notes: The benchmark tests whether agents can use long-term conversational memory to ground tool-call parameters (an offline tool-call generation task). In the main results (§4.1, Table 3) the model is given the ground-truth tool, and only §5.4 tests tool selection with candidate sets N∈{1,2,5}. The paper evaluates 7 memory systems (LTMemory/RAG, SCM, Generative Agents, MemTree, Mem0, LangMem, A-Mem) on Qwen2.5-7B/32B/72B-Instruct at temperature 0, using BGE-m3 for retrieval. The official repo contains only the dataset-construction pipeline (scripts 01-05 plus extract_tool_pool.py, which need an OpenAI-compatible API) and the data files. It has no script that runs or scores the evaluation. The repo has naming inconsistencies: the READMEs refer to Mem2ACT_conversation.jsonl / benchmark_normalized.jsonl and Mem2ACTbench_small/, but the actual files are toolmem_conversation.jsonl and toolmembench_small/. Difficulty levels are given as L1-L4 in the data and main README and as L1-L3 in the dataset README, while the paper defines no levels. On licensing, the repo README says 'MIT License', but there is no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no licence. The data is derived from ToolACE, BFCL and OASST1. The arXiv v1 abstract links an anonymous.4open.science mirror, while the ACL Anthology page links the GitHub repo. Only one arXiv version (v1) exists.

Model calls go through OpenAI-compatible APIs set in utils/api_config.json.

name: PersonaMem-v2

scale.notes: questions = 5,000 benchmark queries (paper 2.4). conversations = 195 persona chat histories in benchmark/multimodal/benchmark.csv, the split the official run scripts and paper-era frontier evals (Fig. 4) use. The text split has 200 personas (a superset) and was used for trained-model evals (Fig. 6). The paper reports only 1,000 personas overall. Averages are per-query means of the total_tokens columns in the multimodal split.

notes: Train/val sizes differ by source. The paper says 18,000/2,000; the HF release, counted 2026-10-10, has 18,549/2,061 (text) and 18,990/2,111 (multimodal). The text and multimodal benchmark CSVs have 5,000 queries each. The multimodal 32k histories hold 183 base64 image messages, but none is tied to a benchmark query: photo-scenario items describe the photos in text. Most official run_*.sh scripts default to --max_items 1000. 128k histories are padded with math/code dialogues. Repo code queries one judge; the paper uses three. Repo has no LICENSE; HF data is CC-BY-4.0. PersonaMem-v3 (arXiv 2608.21381) is a separate paper.

sources.memory_types: arXiv v1 HTML: section 2.2 covers multi-session histories up to 32k/128k (conversational_longterm); implicit user preferences and Figs. 4-5 cover personalization; section 2.3 covers sensitive info and do-not-remember requests, and Fig. 5 reports 'Unlearning' accuracy (memory_security). semantic_knowledge_update dropped: in both HF benchmark CSVs (counted 2026-10-10) every updated=True row is pref_type ask_to_forget ('Do not remember X in memory'; 1,047 text, 1,027 multimodal). No other row has prev_pref. Fig. 5 shows Dynamic and Unlearning at the identical 35.4 +/- 10.5%, so they are the same items. multimodal not tagged: the 195 multimodal 32k histories contain 183 base64 image_url messages (95 personas), but none is the evidence turn (related_conversation_snippet) of any of the 5,000 queries. The 96 pref_type=multimodal items' evidence turns are plain-text photo descriptions with no image attached (also checked in one 128k history).

name: BELA

scale.notes: 40 = random seeds (multi-episode trajectories) of 10 episodes each in main setting (a): same customer, different choice sets. Repo benchmark configs define 40 trajectories x 10 episodes for each of variable_category, variable_persona and variable_settings. No fixed question set. Ablations use 40 or 60 seeds. Pool: 71,088 products, 2,030 categories, 1M personas.

metrics: Regret (best product score minus recommended product score)
Confidence calibration (top-1/top-5 and regret-threshold confidence, ECE)
judge_model: GPT-4o + Gemini-1.5-Pro (averaged persona-product scores that define regret)
notes: The benchmark is interactive and has no fixed question set. A GPT-4o customer simulator answers the recommender, and regret uses persona-product scores from GPT-4o and Gemini-1.5-Pro, so runs need OpenAI and Google API keys (README). The Hugging Face product DB (MIT) lists 1,279,364 products and 7,397 categories (counted on 2026-10-10), versus 71,088 and 2,030 in the paper. The README says 40K+ personas; the paper says a 1M pool. The README title says "Experiential Reasoning". OpenReview lists the paper only as an ICLR 2026 submission.

name: ConvoMem

scale.notes: 75,336 = QA pairs over six categories (User Facts 16,733; Assistant Facts 12,745; Changing Facts 18,323; Abstention 14,910; Preferences 5,079; Implicit Connections 7,546). No single conversation count: each test case mixes 80-120-message evidence conversations with filler up to 2-300 conversations; HF card lists 100 personas, 40,000 filler conversations, plus converted LongMemEval/LoCoMo subsets.

notes: Dataset on Hugging Face is CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial), not gated; code is Apache-2.0. The Scala/Gradle framework calls Gemini/OpenAI APIs, and the ConvoMem evidence files are not in the GitHub repo (download from HF). Paper mentions a judge model without naming it; repo default judgeModel is gemini-2.5-flash. Paper text says ~40% single-message evidence, but Table 2 gives 36,860/75,336 (~49%). README quick-start command does not match build.gradle mainClassName.

name: Evo-Memory

scale.notes: questions = 3,716 is the sum of the per-dataset counts in v2 Appendix F; the paper states no total. Single-turn: 3,320 (MMLU-Pro Eng 969 / Econ 844 / Philo 499, GPQA-Diamond 198, AIME-24/25 30 each, ToolBench 750). Multi-turn: 396 tasks (AlfWorld 134, BabyAI 112, ScienceWorld 90, PDDL 60). No conversations: each dataset is one ordered task stream.

metrics: Sequence robustness (easy-to-hard vs hard-to-easy task order)
Cumulative accuracy / success over the task stream
notes: arXiv only (v1 2025-11-25, v2 2026-05-18). No venue was found. Evo-Memory re-sequences existing public datasets into task streams. As of 2026-10-10 no Evo-Memory code, stream orderings or data had been released. The paper promises a release upon acceptance, and the first author's homepage lists Code as "TBD". v1 also listed Jericho (via AgentBoard), which v2 drops. The abstract says 10 datasets, but v2 names 9. Do not confuse with SakanaAI/evo-memory (NAMM) or EvoMemBench.

name: BEAM

scale.notes: 100 conversations = 20 (128K) + 35 (500K) + 35 (1M) + 10 (10M); 2,000 probing questions = 20 per conversation (2 for each of 10 memory abilities); counted in repo chats/*/probing_questions.json on 2026-10-10. Average turns per chat: 107 / 416 / 842 / 7,757 (paper Table 3).

metrics: Nugget-based rubric score (LLM judge rates each nugget 0 / 0.5 / 1, averaged per ability; 9 abilities)

notes: The paper labels the shortest tier both 128K and 100K. HF dataset 'Mohammadta/BEAM' holds the 128K/500K/1M tiers (90 chats). The 10M tier is a separate dataset (Mohammadta/BEAM-10M). The README gives the answer-generation script as src/model_inference/, but it is at src/answer_probing_questions/. The paper also proposes the LIGHT memory method.

name: MemTrack
venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Scaling Environments for Agents (SEA)

scale.notes: 47 = benchmark instances, each a platform-interleaved timeline (Slack, Linear, Git/Gitea) of 39.9 events on average (max 115). Questions are asked one after another, averaging 3.2 per instance (max 5). The paper does not state a total question count. There is a single evaluation set with no other splits.

metrics: Correctness (LLM-judge score per question, averaged per instance)
Redundancy (fraction of redundant tool calls, LLM-judged)
notes: By Patronus AI. The data is a single Google Drive zip (Memtrak.zip, 294,337 bytes) linked from the paper. Its download endpoint returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-10, but the archive contents were not inspected. No official code repo was found on GitHub, on Hugging Face, or on the Patronus blog. Running the benchmark needs a dockerized environment with Slack, Linear and Gitea servers. The paper evaluates GPT-5 and Gemini-2.5-Pro, each with no memory, Mem0 or Zep, averaged over 5 runs.

name: FlashAdventure

scale.avg_context_length: ~1,142 steps (human average per full story arc; agents capped at 1,000 steps)
scale.notes: questions = 34 games (full story-arc tasks), not QA items. Per §3.4, 27 games have discrete milestones (avg 6.7, range 4-12) and 7 simulation games use a normalized HUD score. Appendix A.5 instead lists 28 discrete and 6 continuous, with Crimson Room at 14 milestones. Each agent gets one run of up to 1,000 steps per game. The judge validation set has 300 samples.

metrics: Milestone Completion Rate (%) (normalized HUD score for simulation games)
notes: This is an interactive GUI-game benchmark with no dataset files. The 34 Flash games are not redistributed and must be installed through the Flashpoint Archive. Copyright stays with the publishers, and use is limited to non-commercial research. The repo (MIT) provides milestone prompts, per-game CUA-as-a-Judge scripts and agent baselines. Runs need a local main display plus Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, and the Docker setup was still marked 'to be updated' on 2026-10-10. Memory is scored only indirectly, through milestones. No human demonstrations are released.

sources.venue: arXiv comment 'EMNLP 2025 Main'. ACL Anthology 2025.emnlp-main.1192 (Proceedings of EMNLP 2025, November 2025, Suzhou, pp. 23354-23384). The repo README says 'accepted at EMNLP 2025 (Main Track)'.
sources.memory_types: episodic: the benchmark targets the 'observation-behavior gap', recalling clues observed much earlier in the same gameplay trajectory and acting on them later (abstract, §1, §3.3, App. A.6.1 with an average gap of 251.1 steps). It is scored via milestone completion. multimodal: agents observe only RGB screenshots (§3.1 POMDP), so the clues to remember are visual. Not embodied: the agent controls a desktop GUI via mouse and keyboard, and the Limitations section notes narrative progression 'does not directly depend on character movements'. Not procedural_workflow: there is no cross-game reuse, and runs are single per game (App. B.1).

name: StuLife

scale.notes: 1,284 task instances, run in order as one simulated academic year. They cover 10 scenarios in 3 modules: In-Class 486, Daily Campus 638, Examination 160. Of these, 554 tasks need long-term memory and 628 need self-motivation. The paper gives no conversation count. Daily Campus subtotals do not match: 637 in the v1 table and 638 in the v6 text, while the v6 sub-scenario counts add up to 639.

metrics: StuGPA (composite out of 100: exam 50, class 30, campus daily life 20)
Success Rate (In-Class / Daily Campus / Exam / Total)
notes: In the main protocol each task is shown as an isolated instance with no history in context. Memory carries over only through the persistent environment state or the agent's own memory or skill mechanism. Grading is rule-based. arXiv has v1 to v6; later versions add more models plus RFT, AWM, Reflexion and memory-augmented baselines. Neither the GitHub repo nor the HF dataset declares a licence. As counted on 2026-10-10, the HF copy of tasks.json (25,149,864 bytes) is a different size from the GitHub copy (24,976,666 bytes).

name: MemoryAgentBench

scale.notes: questions = 2071 total questions for MemoryAgentBench in paper Table 1 (v4). This equals the sum of Table 6 '# of Sequences : QAs': AR = SH-Doc QA 1:100, MH-Doc QA 1:100, LongMemEval(S*) 5:300, EventQA 5:500; TTL = BANKING-77/CLINC-150/NLU/TREC-Coarse/TREC-Fine 1:100 each, Movie-Rec Redial 1:200; LRU = InfBench-Sum 100:100, DetectiveQA 10:71; SF = FactConsolidation-SH 1:100, FactConsolidation-MH 1:100. conversations = null because the paper reports no total. Its units are long context 'sequences' (mostly documents or novels split into chunks and wrapped as user-assistant turns), not natural conversations. The Table 6 sequence counts add up to 130, but the paper never states that total. avg_context_length is the 'Context Depth' range in Table 1. The per-dataset averages in Tables 2 and 6 (GPT-4o-mini tokenizer, 1K = 1024) are: SH-Doc QA 197K, MH-Doc QA 421K, LongMemEval(S*) 355K, EventQA 534K, the 5 classification tasks 103K, Movie-Rec 1.44M, InfBench-Sum 172K, DetectiveQA 124K, FactConsolidation 262K. FactConsolidation also comes in 6K/32K/64K versions. arXiv v1 used a different main set: AR = RULER-QA (2:200), RULER-NIAH-MQ (1:100), InfBench-QA (100:100), LME(S*) (5:300), EventQA (5:500); no DetectiveQA. The Hugging Face splits (Accurate_Retrieval 22, Test_Time_Learning 6, Long_Range_Understanding 110, Conflict_Resolution 8 rows) count context rows, including the context-length variants. They do not match the per-question counts above.

metrics: Accuracy (substring exact match or exact match, depending on task; SH/MH-Doc QA, EventQA, DetectiveQA, 5 classification tasks, FactConsolidation)
notes: The paper tests 4 competencies: Accurate Retrieval, Test-Time Learning, Long-Range Understanding, and Selective Forgetting. v1 called the fourth one 'Conflict Resolution', and the HF split and repo configs still use the name Conflict_Resolution. Most contexts are existing long-context datasets (RULER-style doc QA, InfBench, DetectiveQA, classification sets, ReDial) split into chunks and given as user-assistant turns. The new datasets are EventQA and FactConsolidation (built from MQuAKE counterfactual edits). memory_types mapping: conversational_longterm = LongMemEval(S*); episodic = EventQA (recalling the order of events in novels); semantic_knowledge_update = FactConsolidation (later facts override earlier ones). TTL is not tagged as procedural_workflow or parametric: it is in-context many-shot classification plus movie recommendation from concatenated ReDial dialogues, tested on held-out inputs of the same task, with no weight updates. The dataset composition changed between versions: v2 (Sep 2025) dropped NIAH-MQ and InfBench-QA and added a DetectiveQA subset, and the HF dataset was edited on 2025-07-22, 07-26, 08-05 and 09-29. Pin a revision for comparable results. Licence mismatch: the repo LICENSE and HF card say MIT, but the paper's ethics statement says datasets/benchmark artifacts are released under CC BY 4.0, and third-party sources keep their original licences. Running the evaluation needs an OpenAI API key, and the GPT-4o judge is used for LongMemEval and InfBench-Sum. The repo README points to bash_files/eniac/*.sh, but the scripts are actually at bash_files/sh/*.sh. The README warns that exact_match parsing is strict ('label: 43' does not match '43'). The paper is published at ICLR 2026 (OpenReview id DT7JyQC3MR).

name: MemBench

scale.notes: Counts are the paper's main test set, Sub-dataset 1 (§4.1). Participation has 120 reflective + 360 factual items and observation has 60 reflective + 280 factual items, so the 820 total is a sum of the reported figures. Each item is one trajectory (dialogue sessions or a user message list) ending in one 4-option multiple-choice question; the repo env and data format store one 'QA' per trajectory. Sub-dataset 2 is the noise-extended 100k setting: 30 + 90 participation items (about 100K tokens each) and 15 + 84 observation items (about 10K tokens each), 219 in total. The full released dataset is given in Table 2 as rounded figures (sessions / questions / trajectories / avg tokens per trajectory): PS-RM 3.5k / 3.5k / 3.5k / 2,195; PS-FM 51k / 39k / 8k / 10,285; OS-RM 2k / 2k / 2k / 745; OS-FM 8.5k / 8.5k / 8.5k / 617. It is built on 500 user relation graphs. Per-type breakdowns are in Tables 8-9; the Table 9 caption says 'Participation' but the text calls it the Observation statistics. The released MemData files checked by the registry hold one QA per trajectory (FirstAgent/simple.json has 2 x 500 trajectories), so question counts taken from the files may differ from Table 2.

metrics: Recall@10 (retrieval of key evidence turns; retrieval-based memory only)
Capacity (accuracy as accumulated memory tokens grow)
notes: This is MemBench by Tan et al. (arXiv 2506.21605), not one of the unrelated papers with the same name. It has two scenarios: participation (first-person user-assistant dialogue, repo MemData/FirstAgent) and observation (third-person user message lists, MemData/ThirdAgent). It tests factual memory (single-hop, multi-hop, comparative, aggregative, post-processing, knowledge-updating, single- and multi-session-assistant) and reflective memory (preference, emotion). All questions are 4-option multiple choice scored by exact match. The paper compares 7 memory mechanisms built with MemEngine, mainly on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and also on gpt-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and GLM-4-9B-chat. Noise from a News dataset extends contexts to about 100K tokens. The repo contains the data, generation code and a harness (benchmark/env/Membenenv.py scores accuracy and recall; benchmark/MembenchAgent.py; benchmark/memory/), but it has no runner script. The imported benchutils and utils modules are missing, requirements.txt is only a Git LFS pointer, and the makenoise.py and data2test that the README mentions are not in the repo tree. The README badge says MIT, but the repo has no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no licence. The full data zip (Membenchdata.zip) is also on Google Drive and on Baidu Pan (extraction code yzsj). The Hugging Face dataset mteb/MemBench is a third-party retrieval conversion (source KaLM-Embedding/LMEB), not an official release.

The repo tree (main and neurips_2025 branches) has no file dedicated to the faithfulness/robustness aggregation; src/eval.py computes per-model metrics. WMDP corpora come from a password-protected external zip. Repo supersedes locuslab/tofu; MIT licence.

name: StoryBench

scale.notes: 86 = choice nodes (decision points) in one branching story graph that also has 311 scene nodes, transcribed from the game The Invisible Guardian, prologue to Chapter 5. There are two modes, Immediate Feedback and Self Recovery. Each model gets 10 trials per mode. Self Recovery is split into an original phase and an improved phase of 5 trials each. The paper reports '80+ branching story paths'.

notes: As of 2026-10-10, no official code or data release has been found. The paper links neither, and searches of GitHub and Hugging Face found nothing from the authors. The dataset is transcribed from the commercial game The Invisible Guardian. The paper evaluates Doubao-1.5-pro, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and DeepSeek-R1. In Self Recovery mode the correct answer is revealed after 9 failed attempts at the same choice. The name collides with unrelated benchmarks: YER-hub/StoryBench (text-to-image, NLPCC 2025) and google/storybench (video).

scale.notes: questions = 1,396 tasks (Table 1 '# Instance'): 500 Database (MySQL; selected from 1,306 DeepSeek-R1-generated), 500 Operating System (bash), 396 Knowledge Graph (from GrailQA). name: MEMENTO

scale.notes: 438 embodied episodes in 12 HSSD scenes (Habitat 3.0): 201 memory-acquisition episodes (89 object-semantics, 112 user-pattern), 201 single-memory utilization episodes (same split), and 36 joint-memory utilization episodes (12 object-semantics pairs, 12 user-pattern pairs, 12 mixed pairs). These are tasks, not dialogues, so the conversation count is left empty. The released JSON files match these counts (checked 2026-10-10).

notes: Embodied object-rearrangement benchmark built on PARTNR and Habitat 3.0 with a Spot robot. Agents first complete acquisition episodes, then must use the personal knowledge they gained to handle underspecified instructions. Episode files ship in the repo under resource/datasets/, but the README points to ./data/datasets/. Scenes and assets have to be installed separately through PARTNR's instructions. Only a Dockerfile is provided, not a Docker image. The README citation still uses the earlier v1 title. Code is MIT-licensed.

name: UniEdit

scale.notes: 311,142 = total entries (paper Table 6), each with one edit, one generality and one locality sample (933,426 samples in union). Repo script 16_split_train_test_data.py splits each of the 25 domains into the first 2/3 for train and the rest for test; the paper does not report split sizes. Repo test scripts sample 5,000 test entries per run (-dsn 5000).

metrics: Per-criterion generality/locality scores (Rep, MH, RR, SER, SA, OA; SS, RS, OS, 1-NF)
General capability after 1,000 sequential edits: CSQA/MMLU/ANLI accuracy, SQuAD-2 inverse perplexity
notes: This is a knowledge-editing (model-editing) benchmark built from Wikidata across 25 domains. DeepSeek-V3 generated the prompts and GPT-4 generated the domain keywords. Experiments covered GPT2-XL, GPT-J and Llama-3.1-8B with weight-editing editors (FT, ROME, AlphaEdit, T-Patcher) and external-module editors (SERAC, GRACE, IKE). The Hugging Face data (MIT, not gated) is per-domain dict-keyed JSON, about 2.5 GB train and 1.25 GB test. The dataset viewer/size API failed (checked 2026-10-10).

name: WikiDYK

scale.notes: 77,180 QA pairs over 12,290 facts from Wikipedia DYK entries (Jan 2022 to Apr 2025), covering reliability, generality, paraphrase, portability and locality. There are no dialogues. Facts are injected into model weights by continued pre-training. Table 4's main results inject the full dataset, while Fig. 2 and Sec. 5.3 use subsets of 100, 1,000 or 3,500 facts. Context length is not reported.

metrics: Reported per dimension: reliability, generality, paraphrase, portability, locality
notes: arXiv has only v1 (2025-05-18). The ACL 2026 version is ACL Anthology 2026.acl-long.771. HF YWZBrandon/wikidyk (Apache-2.0, not gated) has 12,290 rows, one per fact, with per-dimension questions in a JSON 'eval' field. The repo's eval scripts instead read a JSON file from YWZBrandon/wikidyk_exp. Questions were generated by LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, o3-mini). Running the evaluation first requires training: facts are injected by continued pre-training using 8-GPU scripts. The benchmark is designed to be extended with new DYK entries.

name: KUP (Knowledge Update Playground)

scale.notes: 6,260 test questions (paper Intro): 2x1K direct-probing MCQs (Update vs. Distractors; Update vs. Old), 4.2K free-form QA (1.1K trigger/impact, 3.1K event details), 60 indirect-probing questions. metrics: Direct-probing MCQ accuracy (Update vs. Distractors; Update vs. Old, with % old fact chosen)
Free-form QA accuracy (LLM-judged; Trigger & Impact, Event Details)
Indirect-probing entailment rate (% responses entailing updated / old knowledge / N/A)
notes: Models are continually pre-trained on the update corpus, then probed (RAG baselines also reported); updates were generated against Llama-3.1-8B/Mistral-7B prior knowledge. HF data (Apache-2.0, ungated) holds only the 5,000 evidence articles; eval questions sit in the repo's non-default `prod` branch (indirect-probing CSV: 64 rows vs 60 in paper, counted on 2026-10-10); MCQs must be regenerated via kupeval/generate_mcq_questions.py. Scripts hard-code the authors' cluster paths; code judge default is GPT-4o vs GPT-4o-mini in paper.

name: PersonaMem

scale.notes: 128k split (the paper's main 15-model evaluation), counted in HF questions_128k.csv on 2026-10-10: 2,727 questions over 60 shared contexts (20 personas x 3). Other splits: 32k (589 questions, 37 contexts, 10 sessions) and 1M (2,674 questions, 31 contexts, 60 sessions). The paper reports ~6k queries and over 180 histories across all versions.

metrics: Accuracy (4-option multiple choice, discriminative setting; overall, per query type, and by session/token distance to the most recent preference mention)
Accuracy in generative setting (option chosen by length-normalized log-likelihood, open-weight models, 32k split)
notes: Questions are first-person in-situ queries of 7 types, each answered by choosing 1 of 4 options. RAG and Mem0 baselines were run on the 32k split. The HF dataset was renamed to bowen-upenn/PersonaMem-v1, and the old URL redirects there. PersonaMem-v2 (arXiv 2512.06688) and v3 (arXiv 2608.21381) are separate, later benchmarks. The released files hold 128 shared contexts in total, against the paper's "over 180 interaction histories". The question_type labels differ between splits. Data and code are MIT-licensed. The evaluation scripts call proprietary model APIs.

name: TiC-LM

scale.notes: No dialogue or QA set. Training data is TiC-CC: 114 monthly Common Crawl dumps (May 2013 to Jul 2024), 2.9T tokens in the training shard, of which runs use 220B or 440B. Evals: TiC-CC held-out (capped at 8,192 sequences of 2,048 tokens per month), TiC-CC-Wiki/News, TiC-Wiki (61 months, 10k changed and 10k unchanged), TiC-StackE (at least 500 questions per period), TiC-CodeDocs (16 NumPy and 11 PyTorch releases).

metrics: Perplexity (token-level ppl_token, answer-level ppl_answer, proper-noun ppl_noun)
DCLM Core average accuracy (static downstream evals)
notes: This benchmark tests continual LLM pretraining: knowledge stored in the weights, measured as forgetting and adaptation across monthly data. The repo releases no eval data, only scripts that rebuild it from public sources (DCLM-Pool/Common Crawl, Wikipedia/Wikidata, StackExchange, NumPy/PyTorch docs). The models README says exact val/test sets are unreleased, so results will not match exactly. Oracle checkpoints are downloadable. Licences: code ASCL, data CC-BY-NC-ND, models Apple TOU. The paper links apple/ml-tic-lm, which now redirects to apple-aiml-research/ml-tic-lm.

name: ImplexConv

scale.notes: 2,500 examples of about 100 sessions each, per the paper. Table 1 lists 255K sessions, 2K average turns and 60K average tokens. Supportive (yes/no) and opposed (open-ended) subsets are scored separately. The paper gives no question count. Counted on 2026-10-10 from the HF dataset-server: 814 supportive × 6 QA = 4,884, and 1,550 opposed examples with about 3,633 QA (mean 2.34).

metrics: Retrieval Accuracy (F1 between retrieved and ground-truth context)
Answer Correctness / Response Accuracy (LLM-judged semantic equivalence to ground truth, plus human evaluation on 100 samples per dataset)
Token Efficiency (average retrieved tokens / token-to-accuracy trade-off)
notes: The paper reports 2,500 examples, but the HF release has 2,364 (814 supportive + 1,550 opposed). The README's HF link redirects to Kaylee0501/ImplexConv-opposed, which holds both JSON files; there is also a separate Kaylee0501/ImplexConv-supportive repo. The HF licence is MIT, and the GitHub repo has none. The paper uses an LLM judge (Code 9 prompt) without naming the judge model. The repo produces responses and retrievals but has no scorer for the LLM-judge accuracy or retrieval F1. Some baseline numbers differ between arXiv v1 and the EMNLP version.

name: MemoryCode

scale.avg_context_length: ~3.20k tokens (short, <15 sessions); ~26.15k tokens (long); longest history 63k tokens
scale.notes: 360 dialogue histories: 30 for each session count of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 40, 50 and 100. They draw on 51 coding instructions (16 can be updated up to 8 times) and 80 fillers. The paper gives no total number of evaluation queries; each instruction has one query, shared with its updates. Short histories are 54% of the set. The dataset totals 4.6M tokens.

metrics: Macro-averaged accuracy (%) of instruction adherence: regex checks on the generated Python code; a sample scores 1 only if every relevant object follows the instruction and the code has no syntax errors. Reported for the Instruction, Session and History settings, with History split into short and long.
notes: Synthetic mentor-mentee dialogues generated with Command R+. The evaluated model acts as the mentee and, given the concatenated history, must apply coding instructions spread across sessions; only the last update of an instruction counts. The repo moved from for-ai/MemoryCode to Cohere-Labs-Community/MemoryCode and ships outputs for 5 models. The HF card config names split 'train' (data/train-*), but the only file is data/test-*.parquet (checked 2026-10-10). Licence: Apache-2.0.

The repo is archived. Code is MIT-licensed and the data is CDLA-2.0.

scale.notes: 15 = test users (3 from each of 5 synthetic communities), each with private documents: user-user conversations, user-AI chats and purchase history. 582 questions: 269 basic, 186 preference, 127 social (Table 2). metrics: Ablation dimensions: preference precision/completeness, noise robustness (F1 drop 0%->70% noise), information updating (1 - share of outdated info)
notes: Only part of the test set is public. Repo data v1 holds 2 of 5 communities: 6 of 15 users and 263 QA items, counted on 2026-10-10. The data was generated with GPT-4o, and the README says it must not be used to develop models that compete with OpenAI. The README's Data link is empty.

name: PrefEval

scale.avg_context_length: up to 100k tokens (configurable; 10 turns ~3k, 300 turns ~103k tokens)
scale.notes: 3,000 = 1,000 unique preference-query pairs x 3 preference forms (explicit, implicit choice-based, implicit persona-driven) over 20 topics. Each pair is used in both a generation task and a 4-option classification task. There is no fixed conversation count: distractor multi-session turns are sampled from LMSYS-Chat-1M and inserted at a configurable number of inter-turns.

metrics: Preference-following accuracy (generation task; absence of all error types)
Error-type rates: preference-unaware violation, preference hallucination violation, inconsistency violation, unhelpful response
notes: Repo licence is CC BY-NC 4.0. The official scripts call models through the AWS Bedrock API, so AWS credentials are required. Data is in the repo under benchmark_dataset/ and also on Hugging Face as three ungated datasets: prefeval_explicit, prefeval_implicit_choice and prefeval_implicit_persona, with 1,000 rows each (counted on 2026-10-10). The paper's judge reported a 5% error rate on 200 manually checked evaluations. The repo also includes SFT training code.

name: QAEdit

scale.notes: 19,249 = QAEdit edit samples (NQ 3,610 + TriviaQA 11,313 + SimpleQA 4,326; ten categories), each with a rephrase and 5 ZsRE locality pairs. Main experiments edit only questions the base model gets wrong: 12,715 (Llama-2-7b-chat), 10,213 (Mistral-7b), 10,467 (Llama-3-8b). Sequential editing uses 1,000 samples per dataset. ZsRE and CounterFact (10,000 each) are also evaluated.

metrics: Token-level accuracy under teacher forcing (synthetic evaluation, for comparison)
notes: The benchmark is QAEdit, a model-editing dataset. WILD ("Without Intervention, Live Decoding") is the paper's evaluation protocol: autoregressive decoding with natural stop tokens instead of teacher forcing. The LLM judge needs an OpenAI API key; without one the repo falls back to exact match. The HF and repo copies of QAEdit.json are the same size (21,042,032 bytes), Apache-2.0, and not gated. WILD was also integrated into EasyEdit (2025-03). The repo additionally ships QAEdit_inter_1k.json, which the README does not describe.

name: REALTALK

scale.notes: 10 real two-person messaging-app chats over 16-21 days (10 participants, each in 2 chats). 728 memory-probing QAs. The paper gives 302 multi-hop, 321 temporal and 111 commonsense, which sums to 734. The released JSON has 301/319/108 (=728), counted on 2026-10-10. Also includes 600 annotated speaker events and a persona-simulation task.

notes: Successor to LoCoMo by the same authors, with real human chats instead of LLM-generated ones. The memory-probing evaluation is evaluate_memory.py, which needs an OpenAI API key. The persona-simulation code is marked 'Coming soon' in the README. The GitHub repo declares no licence, though the arXiv paper is CC BY 4.0. Images are shared in the chats, but the paper captions them with BLIP for memory probing, so the evaluated models see only text. The paper's category counts disagree with the released data (see scale.notes).

name: LongMemEval

scale.notes: questions = 500 manually curated questions across 7 question types (single-session-user, single-session-assistant, single-session-preference, multi-session, knowledge-update, temporal-reasoning, plus 30 abstention/false-premise questions drawn from the other types). conversations = 500 per-question chat histories (haystacks): each evaluation instance carries its own timestamped user-assistant history (paper §3.2 'For each question, LongMemEval compiles a coherent user-AI chat history'; README: 500 instances per file, each with haystack_sessions); histories are compiled from a shared session pool, so they are not 500 independent users. Paper Table 1 reports ~50k total sessions. Three settings with the same 500 questions: LongMemEval_S (~115k tokens/question, main long-context setting), LongMemEval_M (~500 sessions, ~1.5M tokens), and oracle (evidence sessions only). History length is freely extensible via the released compilation script.

notes: Sept 2025: the authors released a cleaned dataset (xiaowu0162/longmemeval-cleaned; files longmemeval_s_cleaned.json, longmemeval_m_cleaned.json, longmemeval_oracle.json) that removes noisy history sessions interfering with answer correctness; the original HF dataset xiaowu0162/longmemeval is marked deprecated, so results on original vs cleaned data are not directly comparable. Data and code are MIT-licensed and not gated. The official QA evaluator (src/evaluation/evaluate_qa.py) calls the OpenAI API (gpt-4o-2024-08-06 as judge; the paper reports >97% agreement with human experts), so scoring needs an OpenAI key. Retrieval metrics skip the 30 abstention questions. The paper's commercial-system pilot (ChatGPT, Coze) used only 97 questions. An earlier version appeared as a poster at the NeurIPS 2024 workshop 'Adaptive Foundation Models'. The authors also released a separate follow-up, LongMemEval-V2 (May 2026, agentic context), which is not this entry.

scale.notes: Each benchmark run is one long conversation. A run has 33 scored tests (11 scenarios x 3 repetitions), and some tests contain several questions. There are six configurations: Isolated (no interleaving) and 2k/32k/120k/200k/500k memory spans. Scores are out of 11, or out of 10 at 2k, where ChapterBreak is omitted. No average conversation length is reported.

metrics: Score: per-scenario scores normalized to [0,1] and summed (max 11; max 10 for the 2k span)
notes: The paper calls it the "LTM Benchmark"; the repo README titles it "GoodAI LTM Benchmark". Paper results use Benchmark 3; the repo also has v1/v2 legacy configs. Tests are generated by code, and pre-generated definitions and results are in data/tests. The smallest v3 config is named 1k in the repo but reported as 2k in the paper. The README cites a root run_benchmark.py, but the file is runner/run_benchmark.py. Evaluation needs the OpenAI API. Licence is MIT; GPT-generated tests are non-commercial.

name: CodeUpdateArena

scale.notes: 670 = program synthesis (PS) examples, the single HF test split (670 rows counted 2026-10-10), covering 161 synthetic API updates to 54 functions in 7 Python packages, with at least 3 PS examples per update. Specificity uses 82 HumanEval instances across 25 random single edits. Table 2 gives only component lengths (docstring 129.0, solution 174.1 tokens) and no total prompt length.

metrics: UPass@k (efficacy: pass@k counting only solutions that pass with the updated API and fail with the old API; @1, @5)
SPass@k (specificity: performance change on a HumanEval sample after editing; @1, @5)
notes: A knowledge-editing benchmark for code. Each instance pairs a fictitious, executable Python API update with program synthesis tasks. The goal is to inject the update into model weights (LoRA fine-tuning) so the tasks are solved without the update docs at inference. Prepending the docs is only an in-context baseline. Evaluation is single-edit, scored by running unit tests. GPT-4 generated the data. arXiv v3 (Apr 2025) still says 'Under Review'. OpenReview lists the ICLR 2025 submission as rejected. MIT licence, ungated.

name: DialSim

scale.notes: conversations = 3 long multi-party dialogues, one per TV show (5 consecutive seasons each of Friends, The Big Bang Theory, The Office). Each one is split into dialogue sessions (scenes): 788 / 805 / 2,347 (paper Table 2). Dialogue length per show is 335,439 / 367,636 / 352,914 tokens (Table 2), about 352k on average (Table 1), with an average of 3.4 speakers. The paper gives no total question count. Table 2 only reports average question candidates per session: 1366.1 / 1306.8 / 497.9. These split into fan-quiz questions (192.9 / 26.7 / 42.7) and TKG questions (1173.2 / 1280.1 / 455.1), or into answerable (1215.0 / 1239.7 / 410.9) and unanswerable (151.1 / 67.2 / 86.9). In one simulation run, at most one question is sampled per session (Algorithm 1). Sessions with fewer than 2 characters are skipped. In the sample, 30% of questions come from fan quizzes and 20% are unanswerable (App. G.1.1). The main results (Table 3) use Friends. The Big Bang Theory and The Office results are in Tables 11 and 12. The data is released in two versions: v1.0 matches the paper, and v1.1 adds unanswerable multi-hop questions (repo README). An adversarial name-swapped version also exists.

metrics: accuracy (correct answers / total questions; mean and std over 3 runs)
notes: The QA dataset behind the simulator is called LongDialQA. In it, the agent plays the main character (Ross / Sheldon / Michael) and must answer questions that other characters ask at random points in a session, using only past dialogue. If it lacks the information, it must answer "(E) I don't know". Character names are anonymized, and an adversarial version swaps names. Questions come in three formats: template multiple-choice, natural-language multiple-choice, and open-ended. The paper's main experiments use multiple-choice. Versions v1 to v5 were titled "A Real-Time Simulator ..." and also tested a response time limit. v6 (2025-09-26) drops the real-time framing. The abstract's "over 1,300 sessions" and "352,000 tokens" are per-show averages; Table 2 gives exact per-show counts. The data is two zip files (dialsim_v1.0.zip, dialsim_v1.1.zip) in a public Google Drive folder. simulator.py loads .pickle files from ./data/. The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub API license: null). Dialogue scripts come from Kaggle and fan quizzes from FunTrivia; the licence for them is not stated. On OpenReview, earlier submissions were withdrawn from ICLR 2025 and rejected from the ICLR 2026 main conference, and an ACL ARR Dec 2024 submission exists. Only the ICLR 2026 MemAgents workshop poster is an accepted venue.

name: StreamBench

scale.notes: questions = 9,702, the sum of the Table 1 test sizes (the paper states no total): Spider 2,147, CoSQL 1,007, BIRD 1,534, DS-1000 1,000, ToolBench 750, DDXPlus 1,764, HotpotQA 1,500. Each dataset is one shuffled stream. There are no conversations, and the paper reports no context length. The HF dataset also hosts train/validation splits for some datasets that are not used as streams.

notes: StreamBench measures how much LLM agents improve over a shuffled input-feedback stream. The only feedback is binary correctness, and the ground truth is never revealed. Here memory is the agent's own store of past instances it reuses, not a recall test. All seven datasets come from existing benchmarks: the CoSQL and BIRD dev sets serve as test sets, and HotpotQA is a 1,500-of-7,410 sample. The text-to-SQL databases are downloaded separately. The repo also has GSM8K and MATH configs that the paper does not use. The HF card gives no licence; the repo is Apache-2.0.

sources.memory_types: procedural_workflow: the benchmark scores an agent by its aggregate metric at the final time step T over a sequential input-feedback stream (paper §2, §3.1). The streaming baselines (GrowPrompt, MemPrompt, Self-StreamICL, MAM-StreamICL; §4.1.2) store past (x, y, fb) in an external memory and reuse it on later, different instances. Not tagged coding_cross_session: the SQL and Python streams are independent single-turn problems with no repo or user conventions, and they use the same generic mechanism as the non-code streams. Not tagged multi_agent_group: the shared memory in MAM-StreamICL is part of a baseline method, not something the benchmark tests.

name: TeaFarm

scale.notes: 100 = TeaBag episodes (sessions 1-5; 50 from MSC, 50 from Conversation Chronicles). 200 = counterfactual QA pairs (2 per episode), each with its own synthesized session 6. The paper reports no context length. In the HF release (counted 2026-10-10), an episode averages about 59 turns (about 1.2K words) across sessions 1-5.

metrics: Success rate (SR): share of counterfactual questions where the agent correctly recalls the past and is not fooled
notes: TeaFarm is the counterfactual evaluation pipeline and TeaBag is its GPT-4-generated dataset. Both come from the THEANINE method paper. The HF dataset (released Aug 2025, ungated, no licence stated) has one 'train' split of 200 rows, one per question, so each episode's sessions 1-5 appear twice. The official repo contains only THEANINE inference code and has no TeaFarm scoring script; the judge prompt appears only in paper Fig. 29. The paper's other metrics (BLEU-4, ROUGE-L, MAUVE, BERTScore, G-Eval, human eval) are for a separate MSC/CC evaluation.

name: LoCoMo

scale.avg_context_length: ~16K tokens per conversation (16,618.1 avg.); ~600 turns (588.2 avg.), up to 32 sessions (27.2 avg.)
scale.notes: Numbers are for the ACL 2024 version and the released data/locomo10.json. conversations = 10 two-speaker very long-term dialogues. questions = 1,986 QA items (single-hop 841, multi-hop 282, temporal 321, open-domain 96, adversarial 446). A registry recount of locomo10.json gives the same 10 conversations, 1,986 QA, 27.2 sessions and 588.2 turns on average. Other annotations: event summarization (35.8 ground-truth events per conversation on average) and multimodal dialogue generation (91.2 images per conversation on average). The only arXiv version (v1) describes an earlier, larger set: 50 conversations, ~300 turns and ~9K tokens on average, up to 35 sessions, 7,512 QA. The repo README says the current release is a 10-conversation subset of those 50, and the repo ships only the 10-conversation file. Separately, 50 automatically generated conversations without human filtering were used only as MiniGPT-5 training data.

metrics: QA answer F1 (partial-match F1 after normalization; per category: single-hop, multi-hop, temporal, open-domain, adversarial, and overall)
Recall@k (retrieval accuracy of RAG models against annotated evidence turns)
Multimodal dialogue generation: BLEU-1/BLEU-2 and ROUGE-L
notes: The arXiv paper exists only as v1 (2024-02-27) and describes 50 conversations and 7,512 QA. The ACL 2024 version (https://aclanthology.org/2024.acl-long.747/) and the public data describe 10 conversations and 1,986 QA, so cite the ACL version for numbers that match the released data. Data is in the repo at data/locomo10.json under CC BY-NC 4.0, so non-commercial use only. Images are not released; the data has only image URLs, BLIP captions and search queries. The observation and session_summary fields were generated with gpt-3.5-turbo and serve as RAG databases. The official scripts cover only the QA task. The README lists event-summarization evaluation and MiniGPT-5 multimodal dialogue generation as 'Coming soon!'. In locomo10.json the numeric QA category IDs do not follow the order in which the paper lists the categories. Matched by count against ACL Table 5: 1=multi-hop (282), 2=temporal (321), 3=open-domain (96), 4=single-hop (841), 5=adversarial (446). The Hugging Face repo adymaharana/locomo, under the first author's account, holds only a README with no data files. Repo last pushed 2024-08-13. A separate re-release, LoCoMo-Refined (github.com/mem-eval-suite/LoCoMo_refined), keeps the 10 conversations, revises part of the QA and uses a stricter judge, so its scores are not comparable to the original.

name: PerLTQA

scale.notes: questions = 8,593 memory-based QA pairs, the full PerLT QA set (paper abstract and Table 2). The paper splits it into train 5,155 / validation 1,719 / test 1,719 (§4.1); the reported experiments use the 1,719-question test set. conversations = 3,409 'event-related historical dialogs' between the AI assistant and the characters, plus 25,256 utterances (Table 2). These dialogues are one of four sources in the memory database, so they are not the unit the QA is organized by. The memory database covers 141 character profiles, 1,339 relationship descriptions and 4,501 events, averaging 313 words per event and 43.7 words per utterance. The paper reports no per-question context length, so avg_context_length is null. The paper says the questions cover 30 characters. The released perltqa JSON files (zh, en and en_v2) have 32 character keys and 8,593 QA items in total: profile 357, social_relationship 897, events 4,501 and dialogues 2,838 (counted from the repo files on 2026-10-10).

metrics: Memory classification: weighted Precision, Recall, F1, Accuracy
Memory retrieval: Recall@K (K=1,2,3,5) and average retrieval time
Memory synthesis/fusion: MAP of memory anchors (exact match of anchors in answer)
notes: There are two versions of the paper. arXiv v1 (2024-02-26) calls the third subtask "Memory Synthesis". The ACL Anthology version (SIGHAN-10, pp. 152-164, Aug 2024, https://aclanthology.org/2024.sighan-1.18/) calls it "Memory Fusion" and describes PerLTQA as a Chinese dataset. The repo ships Dataset/zh (original), Dataset/en and Dataset/en_v2. en_v2 was added on 2025-12-22, and the README says that update fixed inconsistency issues. The paper's results predate en_v2. The paper says 30 characters, but the released QA files have 32 character keys; the total of 8,593 QA items matches the paper. The paper's train/val/test split (5,155/1,719/1,719) is not released as split files. The repo has no evaluation pipeline: it contains only dataset loader classes (Dataset/dataset.py) and a BM25/DPR retriever helper with hard-coded local model paths (memory_retrieval/tools/retriever.py). There is no code for classification, MAP or LLM-judge scoring. All memories and QA were generated with gpt-3.5-turbo and then checked by hand, so the content is fictional. Licence: CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial research only.

notes: DMR is a task inside the MemGPT systems paper, not a standalone benchmark paper. It builds on MSC validation dialogues (Xu et al., 2021). An LLM wrote one question per dialogue whose answer appears only in earlier sessions. The paper never states the question count; the HF release has 500 items. v1 and v2 report different baselines and metrics. The paper does not name the judge model; it only cites GPT-4's agreement with human raters as justification for using an LLM judge. The official repo has no DMR eval script. The HF data is licensed Apache-2.0.

name: MMEdit

scale.notes: 3,093 = E-VQA test (2,093) + E-IC test (1,000) edit samples, summed from paper Table 1; not a total the paper states. Train splits: 6,346 E-VQA, 2,849 E-IC. notes: MMEdit is a knowledge-editing benchmark for multimodal LLMs (edits stored in model weights). The paper evaluates BLIP-2 OPT and MiniGPT-4. It has no conversational component. Its code ships inside the general EasyEdit framework, not as a standalone repo. Data is on Google Drive or BaiduNetDisk, not Hugging Face, and the images are a separate download. In multimodal_edit.py the __main__ block runs a ComprehendEdit training call by default, so the MMEdit test_* functions must be uncommented. arXiv v5 adds EM/Acc results for Reliability and T-Generality.

metrics: Accuracy per evaluation criterion (Logical Generalization, Compositionality I, Compositionality II, Subject Aliasing, Preservation/Forgetfulness, Relation Specificity): a generation (max 20 tokens) counts as correct if any alias of the target object appears in it
notes: The paper (v1 and the TACL version) reports 4,000 edits, but its abstract says "5K". The released repo files hold 4,755 edits (Random has 1,922, not 1,000), counted on 2026-10-10. Results cover only edits that succeeded for each model and method (Table 2). src/evaluation.py samples 200 edits per subset and also instantiates an OpenAI text-davinci-003 executor. The v1 criterion "Forgetfulness" appears as "Preservation" (PV) in v2. The code is MIT-licensed.

name: MemoryBank

scale.notes: 15 = virtual users (ChatGPT role-play), each with a 10-day dialogue history. The histories exist in English and in Chinese (15 users per language). 194 = probing questions reported in the paper (97 English + 97 Chinese). Mismatch: the repo README says 100 probing questions, and the released files hold 100 per language (200 total), in eval_data/en/probing_questions_en.jsonl and eval_data/cn/probing_questions_cn.jsonl. Counted by the registry from the released files (2026-10-10): 15 users x 10 days = 150 days per language, 566 query/response pairs per language (about 38 per user). The English histories average about 2.1K whitespace-separated words per user. These counts come from the registry's inspection, not from the paper. The AAAI version adds that the history covers 450 topics.

metrics: Model Ranking Score (s = 1/r, relative rank among the 3 SiliconFriend variants)
notes: MemoryBank is mainly a method paper (a memory mechanism plus the SiliconFriend chatbot). The benchmark is its quantitative memory-recall evaluation set, released under eval_data/ in the official repo. The paper gives no separate name for this set. Scoring in the paper was done by human annotators, not an LLM judge. The Ranking score only compares the three SiliconFriend variants, so it cannot be compared across other systems. The released probing-question files contain only the question strings, with no reference answers (open issue #22 asks for answers and has no author reply). The repo has no evaluation or scoring script (open issue #17 asks for one and has no reply). The paper reports 194 questions (97 EN + 97 CN), but the repo ships 100 per language. The README's English data links mistakenly point to the cn/ files; the real files are eval_data/en/memory_bank_en.json and eval_data/en/probing_questions_en.jsonl. The repo is MIT licensed, and its last commit was on 2023-05-24.

name: MQuAKE

scale.notes: 3,000 = instances in MQuAKE-CF-3k-v2, the main evaluation subset. Each instance has 3 GPT-generated multi-hop questions (9,000 strings), 1-4 edits and 2-4 hops. The full MQuAKE-CF set has 9,218 instances. MQuAKE-T (real temporal updates) has 1,868. The data is not conversational, so there is no context length.

notes: MQuAKE-CF-3k was fixed in 2024-09 to remove cross-instance knowledge conflicts (MQuAKE-CF-3k-v2.json). arXiv v3 results use v2. The EMNLP 2023 version used the original subset, which is still shipped as MQuAKE-CF-3k.json. The README says MQuAKE-T has 1,825 instances, but the file holds 1,868, matching paper Table 2 (counted 2026-10-10). The official notebook evaluates only MeLLo, loads the v1 subset and calls the deprecated text-davinci-003. Licence: MIT.

Summarization coherence (win rate vs RecursiveSum, human side-by-side)
notes: The arXiv versions leave the dataset unnamed; the DASFAA 2025 version (Springer LNCS 15991) calls it MemoEval. It first appears in arXiv v2 (Feb 2024); v1 only promised a test set. Besides the dialogues (En+Zh, from ShareChat), it has 10 books and 20 VCSum meetings, judged by blind human side-by-side comparison. The data ships in the MIT-licensed GitHub repo. There is no automatic scoring script. The question files also contain SCM model answers.

name: Multi-Session Chat (MSC)

scale.avg_context_length: ~66 utterances per 5-session valid/test episode; avg 1614 tokens (BlenderBot BPE)
scale.notes: conversations = 501 test episodes for each of sessions 2-5 (paper Table 1). Session 1 is PersonaChat: 1,015 test episodes. Test totals: 30,382 utterances and 24,375 summaries. Valid split: 1,000 session-1 episodes, 500 episodes per session 2-5, 31,456 utterances. Train split: 4,000 episodes of 3 sessions plus 1,001 episodes of 4 sessions, 236,987 utterances (Table 1). MSC is a next-response generation task, not QA, so it has no question count. The ~66-utterance figure and the 1614-token average both come from paper §3 'Dataset Statistics'. The 1614 figure is given as an example of context size right after the valid/test statement; the paper does not say exactly which split it covers. Training episodes average ~53 utterances (4 sessions).

metrics: perplexity (per session 1-5 and on session openings)
human eval: final engagingness rating (out of 5)
human eval: rate of referencing own topic / partner's topic / new topic
notes: Human-human crowdsourced English dataset with up to 5 chat sessions per episode. Session 1 reuses PersonaChat, and gold summaries of each session ('extended personas') are included. The task is next-utterance generation, mainly scored by perplexity. It is not a QA benchmark. Data loads through ParlAI '-t msc'. The default teacher covers sessions 1-4 for valid/test; '--include-last-session True' adds session 5. 'msc:PersonaSummary' is the dialogue-summarization subtask. The official tarball msc_v0.1.tar.gz (51,116,516 bytes) redirects to dl.fbaipublicfiles.com and returned HTTP 200 on 2026-10-10. The facebookresearch/ParlAI repo is archived (read-only). Hugging Face copies such as nayohan/multi_session_chat are community mirrors, not official. projects/msc/README.md states no separate data licence; ParlAI code is MIT. Human evaluation used crowdworkers (Mephisto), not an LLM judge.
